title: Benchmark sprint: hybrid deployment & KV/batching tradeoffs - Omega Retail
summary: Technical benchmark sprint kickoff focused on apples-to-apples comparisons across hosted/dedicated/private deployments. Covered KV cache behavior, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, and load generation methodology. Agreed to run synchronized benchmark runs with identical prompts, controlled warm-up, and shared harness. Action items assigned for runbook, prompt set, and scheduling an on-prem pilot cluster for throughput/latency verification.
next_steps: Jordan to share benchmark runbook and loadgen harness link (internal) by 2025-08-18
Customer to provide canonical prompt set (CSV) and traffic mix by 2025-08-20
Schedule on-prem pilot window with Omega infra team for week of 2025-08-25
Redwood SE to provide quantization performance matrix and suggestion table by 2025-08-22
action_items: Jordan Patel; Share benchmark runbook + harness link; Due 2025-08-18
Tom Reyes; Deliver canonical prompt set and typical session lengths; Due 2025-08-20
Maya Liang; Produce quantization latency/quality matrix for their model family; Due 2025-08-22
Priya Singh & Ben Carter; Confirm on-prem pilot infra (GPU types, network, KMS) and availability; Due 2025-08-19
header: Date: 2025-08-11 UTC | Start: 15:00 | Duration: 1h15m | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Aisha (CTO, Omega), Tom (Lead ML), Priya (Platform), Mark (Security), Ben (SRE)
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda, we want to align on methodology for the benchmark sprint and make sure our runs are apples-to-apples. we have a mix of hosted/dedicated/private concerns, so we'll try to nail down variables.
[00:18] Aisha Khan: yeah, we've got exec interest in proof that the dedicated/don't know, on-prem path can hit p95 < 250ms for our checkout flows. curious about how caching interacts with our sessionized prompts.
[00:32] Maya Liang: great, i'll start with the technical framing — i'll call out assumptions up front: same model weights across runs, same tokenizer, same seed for deterministic sampling where relevant, warm-up before measuring, consistent HW profile (we request a pinned A100 80GB for dedicated and equivalent on-prem), and identical batching logic in runtime.
[00:55] Tom Reyes: are we going to measure both open-loop (RPS-driven) and closed-loop (session-driven) workloads? our real traffic is session-heavy with context accumulation so KV cache seems important.
[01:12] Maya Liang: yes, both. we recommend three load patterns: 1) synthetic open-loop uniform RPS to stress concurrency, 2) sessionized workloads that simulate user sessions with prefix reuse to measure KV cache hit curves, and 3) long-tail traffic where prompt length distribution sketches heavier tails.
[01:34] Ben Carter: for on-prem, network egress and KMS calls are a concern. Mark, do you want to say something about encryption needs?
[01:41] Mark Holloway: sure. we need KMS integration with HSM-backed keys, audit logs for every inference request at a minimum meta-level, and zero-knowledge egress rules. if Redwood's private offers support for customer-managed KMS and per-request audit, that's a blocker otherwise.
[01:58] Jordan Patel: noted. Redwood Private supports KMS integrations and audit logs; we'll map the exact API and show sample audit entries. we'll follow up with a security doc link.
[02:08] Maya Liang: back to methodology — caching: there are two levers we care about: KV cache (token-level KV cache keyed by session id) and prefix caching (complete prompt+response pairs). KV cache helps reduce compute for autoregressive decoding by reusing past KV states; prefix caching reduces fetch/compute for repeated templates. in our experiments, hit ratio and cache eviction policy matter a lot. we should instrument hit/miss and time-to-fill stats.
[02:38] Tom Reyes: any heuristics for priming the KV cache? we can't replay every single session.
[02:44] Maya Liang: recommended approach: for sessionized benchmark, replay a steady set of user sessions that match your 90th percentile session length distribution for 20 minutes to warm caches, then start measurement windows. alternative: synthetic prefix priming where we inject the most common prefixes to reach an expected hit ratio prior to run. both should be documented in the runbook.
[03:05] Aisha Khan: quantization is also a big question. we need guidance on int8 vs 4-bit for our transformer family — latency vs quality tradeoff.
[03:16] Maya Liang: we will provide a quantization matrix: for each quant level (fp16, int8, 4-bit) we measure p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput at target batch sizes, and a small eval on your prompt set showing generation divergence metrics (e.g., perplexity delta and token-level edit distance on a sampled set). note: very low-bit quantization reduces memory bandwidth but can add CPU overhead for dequantization in some kernels, so it's not strictly monotonic.
[03:47] Priya Singh: for the apples-to-apples rule, do we pin the same kernel and operator versions? last time we saw differences because runtime selected a different kernel for similar ops.
[03:58] Maya Liang: absolutely. in the runbook we specify kernel versions, CUDA/cuDNN/cufuscation (joke, but you get it), torch/ORT versions, and exactly which runtime flag sets are toggled. we also recommend forcing a deterministic kernel selection or recording the kernels chosen per run so we can compare.
[04:20] Jordan Patel: on batching, we need to decide between dynamic continuous batching vs fixed-size micro-batching. continuous batching increases throughput but raises tail latency. customers with strict p95 SLOs often set an upper bound on queueing latency.
[04:36] Tom Reyes: we care about tail latency. can we get guidance of batch size vs p95 curve?
[04:41] Maya Liang: yes, we'll run sweep runs: for each concurrency level we'll sweep max_batch_size values (1, 4, 8, 16, 32) and plot p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec. also measure queueing latency separately from decode time — we report queue time, KV fetch time, decode time, and post-processing.
[05:02] Ben Carter: what about the KV cache footprint? if we keep large KV caches per session, memory becomes an issue on GPU. do you have eviction recommendations?
[05:12] Maya Liang: we track max KV memory per GPU and recommend LRU with size caps tied to sequence length budget. for on-prem tests we'll ask for the expected max sequence length, and we may enforce an index eviction at e.g., 1.5x expected. we'll also surface percent of sessions that exceed budget so you can choose to truncate or shard.
[05:33] Jordan Patel: real quick — apples-to-apples checklist: same model weights, same tokenizer, same prompt set, identical warm-up length, same HW and kernel versions, same batching policies, documented cache priming; agreed?
[05:47] Aisha Khan: agreed. also document randomness controls for sampling-based generations, or limit to greedy/deterministic passes for latency tests.
[05:55] Maya Liang: yes, for latency and throughput we use deterministic sampling (temperature zero or greedy) unless they want to measure stochastic quality metrics. for qualitative quality tests we run 200 samples with a fixed seed.
[06:08] Jordan Patel: let's talk load generation tools. Redwood has an internal harness (link: internal.redwood.io/bench-harness) and also a recommended open-source tool (link: github.com/redwood/bench-gen) — we'll share both. harness supports sessionized arrival models, token-aware pacing and can replay CSV of prompts with session ids.
[06:25] Tom Reyes: can the harness simulate KV hits by replaying previous responses?
[06:30] Maya Liang: yes, we have a mode to seed KV with prior prefix tokens and also a session-replay mode to simulate incremental sessions. we recommend the following concrete steps in the sprint: seed the cache with 20k sessions derived from your historical logs, run a 10-minute warm-up at nominal traffic, then capture a 15-minute measurement window with both p95 and throughput targets. repeat for hosted/dedicated/private with identical prompt files.
[06:56] Aisha Khan: for on-prem pilot, our infra team uses mixed GPUs (A100 + RTX-based) — can Redwood recommend what to standardize on for fair comparison?
[07:07] Maya Liang: for apples-to-apples, standardize on GPU architecture family (e.g., all Ampere or all Hopper); memory can vary but you need same compute capability. if not possible, we document GPU details and use normalized metrics: tokens/sec per GPU FLOP or latency normalized to a baseline instance. we'll include normalization guidance in the runbook.
[07:29] Priya Singh: what about security posture for the harness runs — can the loadgen run inside our VPC so traffic doesn't traverse public internet?
[07:36] Jordan Patel: yes, for Private we'll deploy an agent inside your VPC that runs the harness and writes metrics back over a secure channel. for Dedicated hosted we can also colocate an agent in a private subnet. we'll include instructions to avoid sending raw prompt texts outside the VPC in the runbook.
[07:54] Mark Holloway: audit logs — we need an immutable log of request metadata for compliance. does Redwood provide request-level tracing and log export to our SIEM?
[08:02] Maya Liang: yes, Redwood Console supports per-request traces and can stream logs to your S3 or SIEM; for Private we can enable direct ingestion or forwarder. we'll show sample JSON schema of an audit entry.
[08:15] Jordan Patel: quick note on observation: instrument KV hit/miss, queue-time histogram, decode-time, batch-size distribution, and batch waiting time. those five will explain most of the variance.
[08:28] Tom Reyes: do you capture kernel-level timelines (GPU op times)? last time a bad kernel selection doubled our p99 because it fell back to a slower op.
[08:36] Maya Liang: we can capture nvprof/ncu-style traces for the run — it's part of the deep dive option. we won't run that by default because it's expensive and noisy, but for the on-prem pilot we can schedule one kernel-level capture.
[08:51] Ben Carter: what about measuring quality regressions introduced by quantization?
[08:55] Maya Liang: short eval plan: take a stratified sample of 500 prompts across your categories, run on fp16 baseline and quantized variants, compute BLEU-ish metrics, token-level edit distance, and a small human review on a 50-sample random subset. report delta and flag regressions beyond thresholds you set.
[09:15] Aisha Khan: anything else we should capture for billing comparability? we want to compare unit economics across modes.
[09:21] Jordan Patel: we'll include tokenized tokens-per-second and GPU-hours consumed; for hosted vs dedicated we'll compute $ per 1M tokens based on your commit vs on-demand pricing and include cost-per-request with and without cache.
[09:35] Tom Reyes: for the on-prem run, do you support MIG-like partitioning or do you need whole-GPU access?
[09:41] Maya Liang: runtime supports MIG for certain architectures; we'll check compatibility with your A100s. runtime can either use whole GPU or configured MIG slices; we note in the runbook differences in throughput and advise avoiding mixed MIG/non-MIG runs in apples-to-apples comparisons.
[09:58] Jordan Patel: socialized schedule: goal is to get inputs by 8/20, SE to prepare quantization matrix by 8/22, then run parallel hosted/dedicated/private runs between 8/25-8/29, aggregate results by 9/2. does that sound reasonable?
[10:13] Aisha Khan: yes, sounds fine. we'll confirm infra availability and get the prompt set.
[10:20] Jordan Patel: ok quick recap of next steps and owners: runbook + harness link (Jordan), prompt set (Tom), quant matrix (Maya), infra confirm (Priya/Ben), security doc (Jordan/Mark). we'll also attach a benchmark sheet template for results collection.
[10:36] Tom Reyes: one quick logistical thing — can we pin the same tokenizer version and share checksums for the model weights? last time we had whitespace/tokenization diffs that changed token counts and muddied apples-to-apples.
[10:48] Maya Liang: yes, checksum the tokenizer vocab and model weights; we also include a small token-count test file. add it to the prompt bundle.
[10:55] Aisha Khan: thanks all, very helpful. we'll aim to deliver the prompt set tomorrow.
[11:00] Jordan Patel: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with links and a rough schedule in email.
[11:05] End of recording (approx).
